report:
## Report

Contrary to the premise, the best current evidence suggests the answer is actually **yes, with caveats** — honey appears to modestly help acute cough in children older than 1 year, though the evidence base is limited.

The Cochrane systematic review (Oduwole et al., updated 2018/2024) compared honey to no treatment, placebo, or over-the-counter cough medicines in children aged 1–18 years with acute cough from upper respiratory infections. It found honey likely reduces cough frequency/severity and improves sleep better than no treatment, and performs similarly to or better than diphenhydramine and dextromethorphan, though the certainty of evidence was low to moderate due to small trial sizes and heterogeneity (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children).

A more recent independent systematic review (2023, European Journal of Pediatrics) reached a similar conclusion: "low quality evidence that honey may be more effective than cough medication or placebo/no treatment in relieving symptoms and improving sleep," while calling for higher-quality blinded RCTs (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/). Mayo Clinic summarizes trial data showing honey performs comparably to diphenhydramine (https://www.mayoclinic.org/symptoms/cough/expert-answers/honey/faq-20058031).

Important caveat: honey must **never** be given to infants under 12 months, due to risk of infant botulism from Clostridium botulinum spores — a consistent, well-established safety warning from CDC and other pediatric health authorities (https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html).

**Conclusion:** For children over age 1, honey likely provides modest, low-certainty benefit for acute cough symptoms and sleep, outperforming placebo and some medications—so the evidence leans "yes," not "no," though better trials are needed. For infants under 1, honey is unsafe and unrelated to efficacy debates.
